subject: Biology
title: Sharks: Apex Predators
description: A 60-second lesson on Sharks: Apex Predators.

hook.text: Sharks have survived five mass extinctions. They've been perfecting their design for 450 million years.

buildup.text: Electroreceptors in their snouts detect the electrical fields of prey heartbeats from meters away.

discovery.text: Sharks regulate fish populations from the top down—keeping prey species healthy through selective predation.

twist.text: Humans kill about 100 million sharks per year. Sharks kill about 10 humans. We're the real predator.

climax.text: Removing sharks triggers trophic cascades—overgrazing by prey species that destroys seagrass and reefs.

punchline.text: 450 million years of evolution. We nearly ended it in 50.

quiz.question: How do sharks detect hidden prey?
options: Electroreceptors sense electrical fields from heartbeats

details.summary: Sharks have patrolled the oceans for over 450 million years, predating dinosaurs by 200 million years. As apex predators, they regulate marine food webs from the top down. Their cartilaginous skeletons, electroreception, and multiple rows of teeth are remarkable evolutionary adaptations.
details.whyItMatters: Shark populations have declined by over 70 percent in 50 years due to overfishing, primarily for shark fin soup. Losing these apex predators disrupts marine ecosystems and costs economies the ecotourism revenue healthy shark populations generate.
takeaways: Sharks predate dinosaurs, surviving for over 450 million years
Global shark populations have declined over 70 percent since 1970
Sharks detect electric fields through sensory organs called ampullae of Lorenzini

faq.question: Why have sharks been so successful for 450 million years?
faq.answer: Cartilaginous skeletons are lighter than bone, providing energy-efficient swimming. Their diverse sensory systems detect prey across multiple modalities. Replaceable teeth ensure they never lose their cutting edge. These adaptations survived five mass extinctions.

faq.question: Are sharks dangerous to humans?
faq.answer: Shark attacks kill about 5 people per year on average, while humans kill approximately 100 million sharks annually. Most shark species are harmless. The fear of sharks is vastly disproportionate to the actual risk, which is far lower than lightning strikes.
